title: Two-Clustering Regime of Token Dynamics in Causal Attention
claim: Under the studied dynamics, tokens spread uniformly at the start collapse into two opposing clusters rather than a single one.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, circles-to-squares marker change
description: Two scatter plots sit side by side with matching axes from -1.5 to 1.5. A faint gray circle of radius about 1.41 appears in both. Panel (a), "Initial positions", shows about 60 small colored circles with black outlines. They are scattered fairly evenly around the circle, and the colors are mixed. Panel (b), "Final positions", shows the same tokens as larger colored squares. They have collapsed into two tight clusters at roughly opposite points on the circle. One cluster is at upper right, near (1.3, 0.55), and the other is at lower left, near (-1.35, -0.4). One isolated blue square sits near (1.4, -0.05). The eye goes first to the dispersed ring on the left, then to the two dense clusters on the right. The contrast between spread-out circles and clumped squares carries the message. Captions are in large serif type below each panel.
caption: Initial (circles) and final (squares) token positions after processing through weight-sharing causal GQA with RMSNorm blocks. Tokens organize into two opposing clusters on the circle.
abstract: We partially resolve Conjecture 1 of [Karagodin et al., Clustering in Causal Attention Masking (NeurIPS 2024)] and extend it to time-dependent parameter regimes. The conjecture predicts that causal attention dynamics converge to two clusters aligned with the eigenvectors associated with the largest eigenvalue $Î»_{\max}$ of the value transformation. We prove that this behavior holds when $Î»_{\max}>0$ and is generally false when $Î»_{\max}\le0$. The resulting two-cluster regime is common in practice and substantially more challenging than the classical single-cluster setting studied previously. A central contribution of our work is the identification of a rigorous dimension reduction phenomenon: despite evolving in a high-dimensional embedding space, token trajectories collapse onto a two-dimensional structure governed by a small number of dominant directions. Building on this insight, we introduce a new analytical framework--instability within the flow--inspired by instability phenomena in physical systems. This framework enables the analysis of steady-regime behavior in non-monotone, non-autonomous attention dynamics. Our theoretical findings are illustrated through simulations and experimental studies using Group Query Attention (GQA) layers.
